diagnostic_evidence.quote: A sequence $\Scal = \{\bsx_0, \bsx_1, \dots\} \subset [0,1)^d$ is called a \textit{$(t,\bse,d)$-sequence in base $b$} if, for any $m,r \in \NN_0$, the point set $\{\bsx_{rb^m}, \dots, \bsx_{(r+1)b^m-1}\}$ is a $(t,\bse,m,d)$-net.
The proof proceeds similarly to the case of $(t,d)$-sequences \cite{Ow95} and is therefore omitted.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that preserving the $(0,\bse,d)$-sequence property requires scrambling whole digit blocks and that standard digitwise scrambling fails to achieve this feat. Both parts are false. The $(0,\bse,d)$ property is purely a statement about point counts in mixed-base elementary intervals, i.e., about which points agree on their first $e_jk_j$ base-$b$ digits in each coordinate. A nested digitwise scramble in base $b$ (Owen's scrambling or the affine matrix scramble) applies to digit $k$ a permutation depending only on digits $1..k-1$, so two points agree on their first $L$ base-$b$ digits after scrambling if and only if they agreed before; hence it preserves the counts in every mixed-base $(b^{e_1},\dots,b^{e_d})$ elementary interval, block by block, and therefore preserves the $(0,\bse,d)$-sequence property. This is exactly the Ow95-style agreement-preservation mechanism the paper itself invokes for Proposition prop:added-1. What digitwise scrambling does not provide is the mixed-base pair uniformity underlying the coarse-base gain-coefficient analysis, which is the true distinction of coarse scrambling.

failure_location.quote: scrambling entire blocks of digits is the natural and necessary way to maintain this structure—a feat not achieved by standard digitwise scrambling

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Reword the motivation: digitwise scrambling also preserves the $(0,\bse,d)$ point-set structure; the advantage of coarse scrambling is that the scramble itself acts on the mixed-base digits, which yields the coarse-base variance analysis and the $O(\log d)$ gain bound.
issues.overall_effect: The paper's stated motivation and novelty attribution are unreliable: block-wise scrambling is not necessary to maintain the $(0,\bse,d)$ structure, and standard digitwise scrambling does maintain it. No formal result relies on this sentence.
issues.title: Introduction falsely claims standard digitwise scrambling does not preserve the (0,e,d)-sequence structure
issues.why_classification: A local rewording of one motivational sentence; every theorem, guarantee, and the paper's actual contribution survive unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Any generalized Niederreiter sequence in prime power base $b$ with the base polynomials $p_1(x),\dots,p_d(x)$ is a $(t,d)$-sequence with $t = \sum_{j=1}^d (\deg(p_j) - 1)$.
every elementary $(k_1, \dots, k_d)$-interval in base $(b^{e_1},\dots,b^{e_d})$ with $e_1k_1 + \cdots + e_dk_d \le m-t$ contains exactly $b^t$ points of $P$
the notion of a $(0,\bse,d)$-sequence in base $b$ is identical to that of an equidistributed sequence in base $(b^{e_1}, \dots, b^{e_d})$

issues.failure_explanation: In both net definitions, the whole cube $[0,1)^d$ is an elementary $(0,\dots,0)$-interval and satisfies $0 \le m-t$ whenever $m \ge t$, so the definition demands it contain exactly $b^t$ points; but it contains all $b^m$ points of $P$. Hence for $m > t$ no $(t,m,d)$- or $(t,\bse,m,d)$-net exists, and since a $(t,d)$- or $(0,\bse,d)$-sequence must satisfy the condition for every $m$, no such sequence exists at all. Under the definitions as written, Theorem thm:t-val-nied and Theorem thm:added-1 are false (they assert specific sequences satisfy an unsatisfiable property), the claimed identity between $(0,\bse,d)$-sequences and equidistributed sequences in base $(b^{e_1},\dots,b^{e_d})$ fails (the left class is empty while instances exist on the right), and every result hypothesizing a $(0,\bse,d)$-sequence becomes vacuous. The standard definition requires $k_1+\cdots+k_d = m-t$ (volume $b^{t-m}$) with exactly $b^t$ points, or equivalently exactly $b^{m-k_1-\cdots-k_d}$ points when '$\le$' is used.

failure_location.quote: every elementary $(k_1, \dots, k_d)$-interval in base $(b,\dots,b)$ with $k_1 + \cdots + k_d \le m-t$ contains exactly $b^t$ points of $P$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Correct both net definitions to the standard form: replace '$k_1+\cdots+k_d \le m-t$ contains exactly $b^t$ points' by '$k_1+\cdots+k_d = m-t$ contains exactly $b^t$ points' (equivalently '$\le m-t$ contains exactly $b^{m-k_1-\cdots-k_d}$ points'), and analogously with $e_1k_1+\cdots+e_dk_d$ for $(t,\bse,m,d)$-nets. All subsequent statements then hold as intended.
issues.overall_effect: The paper's central structural notions are vacuous as defined; Theorems thm:t-val-nied and thm:added-1 are false as stated; cor:maxgain_uk, cor:added-2, thm:added-3 and cor:added-4 have unsatisfiable hypotheses, and cor:added-3's proof premise (that Sobol'/Niederreiter sequences are $(0,\bse,d)$-sequences) fails.
issues.title: Definitions of (t,m,d)-nets and (t,e,m,d)-nets with '<= m-t' and 'exactly b^t points' are vacuous, making thm:t-val-nied false as written
issues.why_classification: The repair is a local, forced correction of two definition displays (the textbook definition, also pinned down by the paper's own equidistributed-sequence correspondence); no claim, rate, or scope changes.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: where all $\pi_{\bullet}$ and $\pi_{\bullet\xi_1 \xi_2 \dots \xi_{k-1}}$ are chosen from permutations on $\Zb$ and are mutually independent

Each $M_j$ is a block lower-triangular matrix with block size $e_j$, where diagonal blocks are drawn uniformly from the nonsingular matrices in $\mathbb{F}_b^{e_j \times e_j}$, and off-diagonal blocks are drawn uniformly from all matrices in $\mathbb{F}_b^{e_j \times e_j}$.
let $\tilde{P}_n$ be its randomly scrambled version using a nested scramble with two-fold uniformity

issues.failure_explanation: The paper's definition of a nested scramble requires the permutations $\pi_{\bullet\xi_1\dots\xi_{k-1}}$ (on $\mathbb{Z}_{b^{e_j}}$ in the mixed-base setting) to be mutually independent. In the block affine matrix scramble, the permutation applied to the $k$-th digit block given a prefix is $y \mapsto D_k y + c_{\mathrm{prefix}}$, where the nonsingular diagonal block $D_k$ and the shift $\Delta_k$ are shared by all prefixes. For example, for input pairs $(x,x')$ and $(\hat x,\hat x')$ that agree within each pair on block $k$ but have different block-$(k-1)$ prefixes, the output differences $\eta_k(x)-\eta_k(x')$ and $\eta_k(\hat x)-\eta_k(\hat x')$ are the same function $D_k(y-y')$ of the shared $D_k$, so the prefix permutations are strongly correlated rather than independent. Hence the block affine matrix scramble is not a nested scramble in the defined sense, and 'two-fold uniformity', which the paper defines only via the permutations constituting a nested scramble, is not literally applicable to it. The lemma's proof is omitted and no proof can exist for the stated claim. Consequently the block affine matrix scramble—the paper's suggested implementation of coarse scrambling, used in the experiments—falls outside the class of scrambles to which Proposition prop:added-1 and Theorem thm:added-2 (and the variance corollaries built on it) are stated to apply. (The intended distributional properties do hold, but establishing them requires an argument the paper does not supply.)

failure_location.quote: the block affine matrix scramble in base $\bsb = (b^{e_1}, \dots, b^{e_d})$ is a nested scramble in base $\bsb$ and has two-fold uniformity

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the false lemma by a direct statement and proof that the block affine matrix scramble (i) preserves digit-block agreement patterns, hence equidistribution (e.g., via preservation of the row spaces of the generating matrices under block lower-triangular nonsingular maps), and (ii) gives each pair of distinct inputs the same joint output law as a fully nested scramble in base $\bsb$ (two-fold uniformity at the first differing block, independent uniform blocks beyond); then verify that the proofs of prop:added-1 and thm:added-2 use only these properties, or cite/provide the corresponding extension (in the spirit of Owen 2003).
issues.overall_effect: The formal guarantees (equidistribution preservation, the variance decomposition eq:variance-gain, and the gain/variance corollaries) are not established for the block affine matrix scramble implementation; they remain valid for fully nested coarse scrambling. The abstract's claim that 'this method' provably achieves the stated rates is unsupported for the suggested implementation as written.
issues.title: Lemma lem:added-1 falsely asserts the block affine matrix scramble is a nested scramble
issues.why_classification: The false lemma cannot be repaired by a local edit: restoring the bridge from the theory to the suggested block-scramble implementation requires a contained but nontrivial argument; no substantive guarantee need be lost.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\sum_{i'=0}^{n-1} \chi(\text{$\bsx_i$ and $\bsx_{i'}$ are in the same elementary $(\bsk + \bsone_v)$-interval})

issues.failure_explanation: The definition of $C$ (eq:C_def) carries a factor $1/n^2$ and that of $\widetilde G$ (eq:Gtilda_def) a factor $1/n$, but the identity eq:Gtilda_formula, the formula eq:Cformula asserted in Lemma lem:Cformula, and every subsequent proof use unnormalized double sums. Expanding eq:Gtilda_def gives $\widetilde G = \frac1n\sum_v H_{u,v}\sum_{i,i'}\chi(\cdot)$, so eq:Gtilda_formula is compatible only with $C = \frac1n\sum\sum\chi$, not with eq:C_def's $1/n^2$; and the proof of lem:Cformula derives $C = t(q+1)^2 + (m-t)q^2$ with no factor at all, contradicting the definition it cites (e.g., for $n = m_{u,v,\bsk}$, eq:C_def gives $C = 1/n$ while eq:Cformula gives $C = n$). Moreover, keeping eq:Gtilda_def's $1/n$ together with eq:G_Gtilde would make item (i) of thm:mimic read $G_{u,\bsk}(n) = 1/n$ rather than $1$ for $1 \le n \le m_{u,\emptyset,\bsk}$, and eq:variance-gain would be false. The convention forced by the proofs of thm:mimic and cor:maxgain_uk and by the MC-baseline normalization ($G=1$) is that $\widetilde G$ and $C$ are plain double sums and $G = \frac1n\prod_{j\in u}(b_j-1)^{-1}\widetilde G$.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Delete the spurious factor $1/n^2$ in eq:C_def and the spurious factor $1/n$ in eq:Gtilda_def, so that $C$ and $\widetilde G$ are the plain double sums used in eq:Gtilda_formula, eq:Cformula, and all proofs; with eq:G_Gtilde unchanged, all subsequent results then hold as intended.
issues.overall_effect: As written, every gain-coefficient statement is false by a factor of $n$: eq:Cformula in lem:Cformula, the exact values in thm:mimic, the equality cases of cor:gain-0ed, the identity $\max_n G_{u,\bsk}(n) = \Gamma_u$ of cor:maxgain_uk, the variance decomposition eq:variance-gain of thm:added-2, and the variance bounds and rates derived from them (cor:added-1, cor:added-2, cor:added-3, thm:added-3, cor:added-4) do not hold under the stated definitions.
issues.title: Mutually inconsistent normalization of C (eq:C_def) and G-tilde (eq:Gtilda_def) versus eq:Gtilda_formula, eq:Cformula, and all proofs
issues.why_classification: Resolving the three mutually inconsistent normalizations (definitions vs. cited formula vs. proofs) requires a nontrivial consistency analysis, and as written the central gain and variance results are false by factors of $n$; nevertheless the repair is local, needs no new lemma, and preserves every claim.

issues.failure_explanation: Item (iv) is false and contradicts items (i) and (ii) of the same theorem. Take $u$ a single coordinate of an equidistributed sequence in base $b_j = 2$ and $\bsk' = (1)$, $n = 2$: item (i) gives $G_{u,\bsk'}(2) = 1$ (since $2 = m_{u,\emptyset,\bsk'}$), while item (ii) gives $G_{u,\bsk'}(4) = 0$ (since $4 = m_{u,u,\bsk'}$), so item (iv) asserts $0 = 1$. The identity that the carried-over argument supports—and that the definition of $\bsk'$ in the statement evidently prepares for—is $G_{u,\bsk'}(nb_j) = G_{u,\bsk}(n)$: under $n \mapsto nb_j$ both sides of eq:Cformula scale by $b_j$ while $m_{u,v,\bsk} \mapsto m_{u,v,\bsk}/b_j$, i.e., scaling $n$ by $b_j$ shifts the level index in coordinate $j$ down by one.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate item (iv) as $G_{u,\bsk'}(nb_j) = G_{u,\bsk}(n)$ for $\bsk'$ with $k'_j = k_j+1$ and $k'_\ell = k_\ell$ ($\ell \ne j$), a direct consequence of eq:Cformula.
issues.overall_effect: Item (iv) of thm:mimic is false as stated; it is not used elsewhere in the paper, so no other result is affected.
issues.title: thm:mimic item (iv): the invariance $G_{u,\bsk'}(nb_j) = G_{u,\bsk'}(n)$ is false
issues.why_classification: A local correction of one displayed identity in one theorem item; the corrected identity is of the same strength, nothing downstream uses the item, and no proof architecture changes.

issues.failure_explanation: Item (v) is false and contradicts items (ii) and (i) of the same theorem. For a single coordinate in base 2 and $\bsk = \bszero$, item (ii) gives $G_{u,\bszero}(2n) = 0$ for every $n$ (since $2n = n\,m_{u,u,\bszero}$), whereas item (i) gives $G_{u,\bszero}(1) = 1$, so item (v) asserts $0 = 1$ at $n = 1$. It also fails for nonzero $\bsk$: for $\bsk = (4)$ and $n = 7$, item (i) gives $G_{u,\bsk}(14) = 1 \ne 1/7 = G_{u,\bszero}(7)$. The identities supported by the scaling of eq:Cformula are $G_{u,\bsk}(n\prod_{j\in u}b_j) = G_{u,\bsk-\bsone}(n)$ (for $\bsk \ge \bsone$) and, equivalently, $G_{u,\bsk}(n\,m_{u,\emptyset,\bsk}) = G_{u,\bszero}(n)$ for all $\bsk$; the stated version conflates the two.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate item (v) correctly, e.g., as $G_{u,\bsk}(n\,m_{u,\emptyset,\bsk}) = G_{u,\bszero}(n)$ for all $\bsk \in \NN_0^{|u|}$, or as $G_{u,\bsk}(n\prod_{j\in u}b_j) = G_{u,\bsk-\bsone}(n)$ for $\bsk \ge \bsone$.
issues.overall_effect: Item (v) of thm:mimic is false as stated; it is not used elsewhere in the paper, so no other result is affected.
issues.title: thm:mimic item (v): the identity $G_{u,\bsk}(n\prod_{j\in u}b_j) = G_{u,\bszero}(n)$ is false
issues.why_classification: A local correction of one displayed identity; the corrected identity is comparably strong, no downstream result uses the item, and no other proof changes.
